explanations.explanation: Moab it is, friend. The verse says the man, his wife and his two sons “…went to reside in the land of Moab.” (Ruth 1:1) A whole family packs up and heads for a new country. I've packed for a trip before, and I always forget something, usually my own hat.

Egypt isn't in this verse, friend. The text says the family went to reside in the land of Moab. Then verse 2 says they entered Moab and settled there (Ruth 1:2). One country in the verse, and it isn't Egypt.

Edom doesn't show up in this verse, friend. The family goes to the land of Moab, and verse 2 says they settled there (Ruth 1:2). Easy to mix up when you're hearing a lot of unfamiliar names. Moab is the one the text gives.

Ruth, friend. The verse says the sons took Moabite women as their wives, “…one named Orpah and the other named Ruth.” (Ruth 1:4) Remember that name, because this whole book carries it. She's about to make some big choices.

Rachel isn't one of the women in this story, friend. The sons took Moabite women as wives, “…one named Orpah and the other named Ruth.” (Ruth 1:4) Ruth is the name this book is named after. Keep it in your apron pocket.
Dinah isn't in this passage, friend. The two Moabite women the sons married are Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Ruth is the one to hold onto. You'll be hearing a lot more about her.

Yes, friend, and this part is heavy. The text says both Mahlon and Chilion died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband (Ruth 1:5). Her husband Elimelech had already died, so now it's just Naomi. No joke here, because this loss is real.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a fire, friend. What it says is heavier: Mahlon and Chilion both died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband (Ruth 1:5). I'll skip the jokes on this one. It's a hard verse.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text, friend. The verse says both Mahlon and Chilion died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband (Ruth 1:5). Nothing is said about her eyes. This is a heavy part of the story, so I'll let it be heavy.

Food, friend. The text says Naomi heard in Moab “…that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food.” (Ruth 1:6) The story opened with a famine, so this is real news. I know how it feels to hear good news after a long stretch of bad.

No king in this verse, friend. Naomi hears that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food (Ruth 1:6). The story started with a famine, so food is the news. Anybody who's been hungry knows that's big news.
Victory isn't what the verse says, friend. Naomi hears that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food (Ruth 1:6). No battle in sight. This one is about the famine ending.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Naomi tells them, “Go back, each of you to your mother's home.” (Ruth 1:8) She's telling both of them to turn around, even though they came this far with her. Orpah and Ruth are the two women who married her sons.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Nothing about the dark in this verse, friend. Naomi tells her daughters-in-law, “Go back, each of you to your mother's home.” (Ruth 1:8) She's sending them home, not speeding them up. I'd have just said 'hurry up,' and I'd have gotten it wrong too.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: It's the opposite, friend. Naomi tells Orpah and Ruth, “Go back, each of you to your mother's home.” (Ruth 1:8) She's the one sending them away, not holding them close. Orpah and Ruth walked this far with her, and now she turns them around.

True, friend. Naomi says, “May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” (Ruth 1:9) She's speaking a blessing over both women. And that's what comes right before the kiss and the tears.

That one's true, friend. Naomi says, “May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” (Ruth 1:9) It's right there in her send-off. She speaks it over both women, and then the tears start.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. They say, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10) Naomi just tried to send them home, and both women answer by saying they're going with her. That's loyalty with tears on it.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: They say the opposite, friend. Orpah and Ruth tell Naomi, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10) Staying put is not what they offer. They want to go with her.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Not a visit, friend. They say, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10) That's a lot more than dropping by. Both women say they're coming with her, not meeting her later.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Naomi asks, “…would you wait for them to grow up?” (Ruth 1:13) She's laying out the case to turn them back. And you'll notice she asks it twice in a row, because she is not letting this one go.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not her question, friend. Naomi asks, “…would you wait for them to grow up?” (Ruth 1:13) She says even if she had hope for sons tonight, she wonders if they'd wait. Raising them is not in the verse.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Bethlehem isn't in her question, friend. Naomi asks, “…would you wait for them to grow up?” (Ruth 1:13) She's talking about the sons she says she can't have, and whether they'd wait. It's a hard question, and she means it.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: That's what she says, friend. Naomi says it's much more bitter for her “…because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” (Ruth 1:13) Those are her words, and she's speaking from a lot of pain. I think this is a woman who's hurting, and I'll leave it there.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Judah isn't her reason, friend. Naomi says it's much more bitter for her “…because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” (Ruth 1:13) She doesn't mention anybody in Judah turning on her. She's pointing at the LORD's hand, and that's all the text gives.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: She never says that, friend. Naomi says it's much more bitter for her “…because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” (Ruth 1:13) Nothing about the people of Moab. She names the hand of the LORD.

True, friend. The text says, “…Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.” (Ruth 1:14) Orpah says her goodbye with a kiss. And notice that little word 'but,' because it's about to split the road in two.
That one's true, friend. The text says, “…Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.” (Ruth 1:14) So Orpah does kiss Naomi goodbye. Ruth is the one who clings.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “…Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.” (Ruth 1:14) Orpah is the one who kisses Naomi goodbye. Ruth doesn't leave with her.

False, and you read that right, friend. The text says, “…Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.” (Ruth 1:14) Orpah says goodbye, and Ruth holds on to Naomi. Two women, two choices, one road.
True, friend. Naomi says, “Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” (Ruth 1:15) She's still urging Ruth to turn around. She's not giving up easy.

That one's true, friend. Naomi says, “Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” (Ruth 1:15) So she does tell Ruth to follow Orpah. Ruth is about to answer her.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Ruth says, “…your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” (Ruth 1:16) She doesn't just promise to walk with Naomi. She says Naomi's God will be hers. I could use a friend who talks like that.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: A house isn't part of this promise, friend. Ruth says, “…your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” (Ruth 1:16) Ruth's words are about where she'll go, where she'll live, who her people are and who her God is. That's a lot bigger than a house.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: That's not in her words, friend. Ruth says, “…your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” (Ruth 1:16) She promises that Naomi's people and Naomi's God will be hers. Learning the ways isn't mentioned.

Death, friend. Ruth says, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:17) That's about as strong a promise as a person can make. She's saying only death will part them.

Not distance, friend. Ruth says, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:17) Miles don't break this promise. Death is the only thing she names.

Marriage isn't the word, friend. Ruth says, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:17) Naomi had just talked about new husbands. Ruth answers by saying only death will separate them.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says, “When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.” (Ruth 1:18) After all those arguments, she lets it go. Ruth's mind is made up, and Naomi sees it.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: She had already tried that, friend. Verse 18 says, “When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.” (Ruth 1:18) So after Ruth's promise, Naomi stops. She doesn't send her anywhere.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: No waiting in Moab here, friend. The text says, “When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.” (Ruth 1:18) Naomi stops arguing, and the two of them keep walking. Ruth is going with her.

That's right, friend. The women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19) The whole town is stirred up when the two of them arrive. I think they're surprised to see her, and I'll leave it at my guess.
That's not what they say, friend. The women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19) They're talking about Naomi herself. Her husband doesn't come up in their words.
They don't call her a stranger, friend. The women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19) They know her name and use it. The whole town is stirred, and they say it out loud.

Mara, friend. Naomi says, “Do not call me Naomi… Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20) She asks them to use a new name. Those are her own words about how she feels.

Hannah isn't the name, friend. Naomi says, “Do not call me Naomi… Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20) Mara is the name she picks. It goes with the bitterness she describes.
Leah isn't in this verse, friend. Naomi says, “Do not call me Naomi… Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20) She picks Mara. Hold onto that one.

That one's flipped, friend. Naomi says, “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” (Ruth 1:21) She's the one who says empty, not full. Her words are heavy, and the text lets them stand.
False, and you caught it, friend. Naomi says, “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” (Ruth 1:21) She went out full and came back empty. Those are her words, and she means them.

Barley, friend. The text says they arrived in Bethlehem “…at the beginning of the barley harvest.” (Ruth 1:22) Remember how it all started with a famine? Now there's a harvest coming in, and I'm as happy about that as a dough ball on a warm counter.

Wheat isn't the word, friend. The text says they arrived in Bethlehem “…at the beginning of the barley harvest.” (Ruth 1:22) It's barley. Worth remembering, because that harvest matters for what comes next.
Olive isn't in this verse, friend. The text says they arrived in Bethlehem “…at the beginning of the barley harvest.” (Ruth 1:22) Barley is the crop it names. Keep that in your pocket.
